description:
Wesam Saad begins the Heaven studies by asking how much of our picture of eternity comes from Scripture and how much comes from familiar images, songs and imagination. He establishes a consistent approach to reading biblical prophecy: take the text in its ordinary sense while recognising figures of speech. The accompanying book supplies a framework for discussion, but the Bible remains the authority against which every claim must be tested.

The example of the Bereans in Acts 17:11 challenges listeners to examine even respected teaching rather than accept it automatically. Studying heaven also directs attention to Christ and to the promised life with God, where death, grief and pain will be removed. Remembering the brevity of earthly life helps believers weigh their present priorities against the permanence of their future home.

The practical concern is how this hope shapes holiness and the use of money, time, energy and gifts. Wesam connects expectation of the new heavens and earth with diligent, godly living, while clarifying that entry into heaven rests on Christ rather than earned merit. The session ends by gathering questions for the coming studies. Those questions establish an agenda for exploration, rather than supplying settled answers about every detail of eternal life.

questions.question: Why should familiar pictures of heaven be tested against Scripture?
questions.answer: Pictures formed by entertainment, songs, funerals or imagination can make eternal life seem vague or unattractive. Wesam uses the Bereans as an example of receiving teaching eagerly while examining Scripture. Their care extended even to the apostle Paul, so a pastor, a book or a family member should not become the final authority for beliefs about heaven.

questions.question: What approach to biblical prophecy carries into the Heaven studies?
questions.answer: Wesam argues for the same ordinary reading of the text used when studying biblical history and prophecies about Christ’s first coming. He does not deny figures of speech; readers must recognise them where the text uses them. His concern is that future promises should not receive a different method of interpretation merely because their fulfilment is difficult to imagine.

questions.question: What role does the accompanying book have?
questions.answer: The book provides a framework and ideas for the course, rather than an independent source of authority. Wesam explicitly places Scripture above the book. Its suggestions, like the teacher’s explanations, must therefore be tested against the Bible instead of being accepted simply because they appear in the study material.

questions.question: Why is attention to heaven inseparable from attention to Christ?
questions.answer: The study connects the command to seek the things above with the place where Christ is seated. Christian hope concerns being with him, rather than enjoying an attractive place apart from him. The reading from Revelation also places God’s dwelling with his people at the centre of the promised new earth, alongside the removal of death, grief and pain.

questions.question: How can the brevity of life change the way believers use their resources?
questions.answer: Psalm 39 presents human life as brief and passing. Wesam says that thinking seriously about an eternal home changes the value placed on money, investments, time, energy and gifts. Instead of organising life as though the present world were permanent, believers should consider how their resources can serve God’s glory with eternity in view.

questions.question: How does hope for the new heavens and earth encourage holiness?
questions.answer: Wesam draws attention to the connection in 2 Peter 3:13–14 between looking for the promised future and being diligent to live in peace, spotless and blameless. As the reality of that future becomes more firmly established in the mind, it reshapes desires and priorities. The expectation is intended to influence present conduct, rather than remain an interesting subject for speculation.

questions.question: Does holy living earn a person’s place in heaven?
questions.answer: Holy living does not earn entry into heaven. When the discussion risks making arrival in heaven conditional on a person’s achievements, Wesam clarifies that believers enter through the blood of Jesus. Holiness is evidence of that relationship and an appropriate response to hope, rather than the payment that secures admission. The call to godliness must be kept together with that distinction.

questions.question: How should the many questions raised at the end of the session be treated?
questions.answer: They are topics for later investigation, not a collection of answered doctrinal claims. The group raises questions about bodies, relationships, work, worship and other features of eternal life, while Wesam records what listeners want to understand. His stated aim is to unfold what Scripture teaches and encourage people to leave everything behind and follow Jesus, without claiming exhaustive knowledge of heaven.
